restoration_note: This teaching gives three parallel similes for one Lord at three registers: First Man as a famous man recovering scattered property, the Splendor (ship of days) as a furnace where the wise craftsman forges every armament, the Living Spirit as a warrior drawing the captive king's son out of enemy hands, and the Third Ambassador as a great man bringing his captives' powers of light back. The first simile (sections 1597-1602) is structurally complete and supplied the formula vocabulary — ⲡⲉϩⲭⲣⲏⲙⲁ 'his property', ⲁϩⲉⲓ ⲥⲁ 'came after', ⲭⲣⲁⲣⲉ ⲁⲃⲁⲗ 'scattered forth', ⲥⲁⲧϩ ⲁⲃⲁⲗ ⲍⲛ ⲛ̄ⲟⲓⲭ ⲛ̄ⲛⲉϩⲭⲁⲭⲉ 'draw out from the enemies' hands' — which fixes the formulaic gaps in the parallel similes and the closing Ambassador section with high confidence. Greek loanword completions (ⲧⲉⲭⲛⲓⲧⲏⲥ, ⲡⲁⲛⲍⲟⲡⲗⲓⲁ, ⲁⲓⲭⲙⲁⲗⲱⲧⲓⲍⲉ, ⲁⲓⲭⲙⲁⲗⲱⲧⲟⲥ), Lyc. word-completions (ⲡϣⲁⲣⲡ, ⲟⲩⲱⲏⲣⲉ, ⲭⲁⲗⲙ̄ⲗⲁⲍ, ⲭⲣⲁⲣⲱⲟⲩ), and the correlative formula Ⲧϩⲉ ⲁⲛ ⲧⲉ ⲧⲉⲓ ⲉⲧⲁ- carry the secure gaps. Sections 1610, 1617, 1619, and 1620 are too damaged for responsible restoration; the verb cluster between subject and ⲡⲣⲓⲉ in 1606 is also unrestorable. Two editor readings (ⲁ⳨ⲟⲩⲁⲓ̈ and ⲁⲥⲁⲧϩⲟⲩ) are followed but flagged as low-confidence witness readings rather than confirmed text.
